title: Writing Large Numbers in Scientific Notation

steps.body: Scientific notation writes any number as a × 10ⁿ, where a is between 1 and 10 (1 ≤ a < 10). For large numbers: 45,000 = 4.5 × 10⁴ — move the decimal point left until only one nonzero digit remains before it, and count how many places you moved.
Separate a large number into a coefficient and its place-value exponent.

widget.prompt: Explore the coefficient and place exponent for 320,000,000, then choose its scientific notation.

choices.label: 3.2 × 10⁸
choices.feedback: Correct. The coefficient is 3.2 and the decimal moved eight places, so the exponent is 8.

choices.label: 32 × 10⁷
choices.feedback: That value is equivalent, but 32 is not a valid scientific-notation coefficient because it is not less than 10.

choices.label: 3.2 × 10⁷
choices.feedback: The coefficient is valid, but the decimal moved eight places rather than seven.

widget.successFeedback: 320,000,000 = 3.2 × 10⁸. The coefficient is between 1 and 10, and the exponent records eight place moves.
widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect both the coefficient and exponent stages before selecting an answer.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Place one nonzero digit before the decimal, then count how many places the decimal moved.

predict.prompt: In scientific notation, the coefficient is at least 1 and less than which number?
predict.reveal: A scientific-notation coefficient has exactly one nonzero digit before the decimal, so it is at least 1 and less than 10. The exponent then carries the place-value shift.

steps.body: The exponent counts how many places the decimal point moved. A whole number like 7,000 has an invisible decimal point at the end (7000.), and moving it left 3 places gives 7 × 10³.
Convert a number ending exactly on a power of ten.
explanationVariants: 7,000 = 7 × 10³ — the decimal moves 3 places left, and 7 is already a single digit.
7,000. has 3 zeros; moving the decimal past all three gives 7 × 10³.

commonBuilds.feedback: That's one power too many — 7,000 only needs 3 places.
The coefficient must be 1 ≤ a < 10 — 70 is too big; 7 × 10³ is standard form.
The coefficient must be at least 1 — 0.7 is too small; 7 × 10³ is standard form.

widget.missFeedback: One digit before the point, then count the places: 7,000 = 7 × 10³.
widget.successFeedback: Right — 3 places, and 7 is already between 1 and 10.

commonErrors.feedback: That's 6.1 × 10⁶ — one power too many; 6.1 × 10⁵ moves the decimal only 5 places: 610,000.
That's 6.1 × 10⁴ — one power too few; 6.1 × 10⁵ needs 5 places: 610,000.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 6.1 × 10⁵ means move the decimal 5 places right: 610,000.

steps.body: Apply it: a real rate, converted.
explanationVariants: A quarter million operations is 2.5 × 10⁵, a different exponent class than the millions elsewhere in this lesson.

widget.prompt: A processor completes 250,000 operations per second. Write 250,000 in scientific notation.

commonBuilds.feedback: That's one power too many — 250,000 needs the decimal to move only 5 places, not 6.
The coefficient must be 1 ≤ a < 10 — 25 is too big; 2.5 × 10⁵ is standard form.
Count again — 250,000 needs the decimal to move 5 places, not 4.

widget.missFeedback: Put the point after the 2, then count five places back to 250,000.
widget.successFeedback: Right — 5 places, and 2.5 is between 1 and 10.

steps.body: Spot the flaw in someone else's conversion.

widget.prompt: A city's population is 6,400,000. A student writes this as 64 × 10⁵. What's the flaw, and what should it be?

options.label: The coefficient must be under 10 — it should be 6.4 × 10⁶
options.feedback: Right — 64 isn't a valid coefficient (1 ≤ a < 10). Moving one more place gives 6.4 × 10⁶, the same value with a valid coefficient.

options.label: The exponent should be 6, but 64 can stay as the coefficient
options.feedback: Changing only the exponent changes the value: 64 × 10⁶ = 64,000,000, not 6,400,000. The coefficient has to shrink to 6.4 when the exponent grows to 6.

options.label: Nothing is wrong — 64 × 10⁵ is valid scientific notation
options.feedback: 64 × 10⁵ does equal 6,400,000, but scientific notation requires the coefficient to be between 1 and 10 — 64 is too big. The standard form is 6.4 × 10⁶.

explanationVariants: 5,080,000 = 5.08 × 10⁶ — the coefficient keeps its internal zero, from the 0 sitting right after the leading 5.
The decimal moves 6 places, landing after the 5, but the very next digit (0) stays in the coefficient too: 5.08.

widget.prompt: A stadium sold 5,080,000 tickets this year. Write that total in scientific notation.

commonBuilds.feedback: 5.8 drops the internal zero — the digit right after the 5 is 0, and it belongs in the coefficient too: 5.08 × 10⁶.
The coefficient must be 1 ≤ a < 10 — 508 is far too big; 5.08 × 10⁶ is standard form.
Count again — 5,080,000 needs the decimal to move 6 places, not 5.

widget.missFeedback: Keep every digit up to (and including) the last nonzero one: 5.08 × 10⁶, not 5.8.
widget.successFeedback: Right — the coefficient keeps its internal zero: 5.08 × 10⁶.

explanationVariants: 1,000,000,000 = 1 × 10⁹ — the decimal moves 9 places, landing on exactly 1.
Even though the coefficient is exactly 1, that still satisfies 1 ≤ a < 10 — it's valid standard form.

commonBuilds.feedback: Count the zeros carefully — one billion has 9 zeros, not 10.
The coefficient must be 1 ≤ a < 10 — 10 is too big (right at the boundary, not under it); 1 × 10⁹ is standard form.
The coefficient must be at least 1 — 0.1 is too small; 1 × 10⁹ is standard form.

widget.missFeedback: A billion is a 1 followed by nine zeros: 1 × 10⁹.
widget.successFeedback: Right — 9 places, and 1 is a valid coefficient (1 ≤ a < 10).

hints: How many zeros does one billion have?
The decimal moves 9 places, landing right after the 1: 1 × 10⁹.

steps.body: Large numbers become a × 10ⁿ with a positive n, where 1 ≤ a < 10.
takeaways: Move the decimal left until one nonzero digit remains before it.
The exponent counts how many places the decimal moved.
The coefficient must satisfy 1 ≤ a < 10 — never 10 or more, never less than 1.
steps.teaser: Next: the same idea for very SMALL numbers, using negative exponents.

concept.body: To write a large number in scientific notation (a × 10ⁿ), move the decimal point left until one nonzero digit remains before it; the exponent counts the places moved.

explanationVariants: Counting from 50000., the decimal moves past 4 digits to land after the 5.

options.label: 5 × 10⁴
options.feedback: Right — 4 places, and 5 is between 1 and 10.

options.label: 50 × 10³
options.feedback: The coefficient must be 1 ≤ a < 10 — 50 is too big; 5 × 10⁴ is standard form.

options.label: 5 × 10⁵
options.feedback: That's one power too many — 50,000 needs exactly 4 places.
